title: Seeded SU(1,1) interferometry for Fourier-domain optical coherence tomography
authors: Alejandra A. Padilla, Valentina Gacha, Daniel F. Urrego, Juan P. Torres
abstract: We demonstrate Fourier-domain optical coherence tomography (FD-OCT) based on a seeded SU(1,1) interferometer. Multilayer objects are probed with broadband light centered at 1550nm, while depth-resolved 3D images are reconstructed from photon flux measurements centered at 810nm. We show that, in the low parametric-gain regime, seeding increases the photon flux, enabling volumetric imaging with a spectrometer rather than single-photon detectors. Our analysis further shows that, under the conditions considered, seeding provides a more effective route to sensitivity enhancement than increasing the parametric gain.
summary: This paper presents the use of a seeded SU(1,1) interferometer for Fourier-domain Optical Coherence Tomography (FD-OCT). By implementing seeding, the authors overcome low photon flux limitations inherent in the system, enabling high-flux, volumetric 3D imaging. They conclude that seeding is a superior method for enhancing measurement sensitivity compared to increasing the intrinsic parametric gain.
main_problem: The paper addresses the development of Fourier-domain Optical Coherence Tomography (FD-OCT) using a seeded SU(1,1) interferometer, specifically overcoming low photon flux limitations.
main_result: Seeding the interferometer significantly increases the photon flux, enabling volumetric imaging using standard spectrometers, and this method proves more effective for sensitivity enhancement than increasing parametric gain.
method: The authors combine theoretical modeling of multilayer object reflectivity with experimental demonstration using a seeded SU(1,1) setup to reconstruct depth-resolved 3D images via Fourier transformation of the measured spectrum.
model_or_system: The physical system is an SU(1,1) interferometer utilizing nonlinear parametric down-conversion in a PPLN crystal. It is used to probe multilayer objects by sending broadband light at 1550 nm and measuring reflected signals at 810 nm.
key_observables: Reconstructed axial scans (A-scans) showing internal layer composition, and the measured photon flux $\langle N_{s2} angle$ used for precision estimation.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the low parametric gain regime necessitates seeding for practical high-flux measurements, and certain simplifications are made regarding the object reflectivity in the idler path.

paper_structure: The paper moves from establishing the experimental setup and theory (including OCT requirements and sensitivity decay correction) to demonstrating the successful application of seeding for high-flux, high-resolution volumetric imaging.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems as it details the practical implementation of quantum-enhanced sensing (via nonlinear interferometry) for advanced imaging applications, specifically quantifying the advantage of seeding over simply increasing parametric gain.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Experimental setup to demonstrate Fourier-domain optical coherence tomography using a seeded SU(1,1) interfer- ometer. Signal (s1) and idler (i1) photons are generated via non-degenerate parametric down-conversion. The idler photons probe the sample. Photons reflected from the sample, together with the reflected pump (p) and signal photons, are re-injected into the nonlinear crystal. The interferometer can operate in two configurations: (a) unseeded, where detection is performed using single-photon detectors, and (b) seeded, where a broadband superluminescent diode (SLD) increases the photon flux rate, enabling detection with a spectrometer. Peaks correspond to reflections from refractive-index discontinuities within the samples. The reported thicknesses d are extracted from the peak separations using ∆z = 2ngd, with ng = 1.5. Manufacturer-specified thicknesses are: (a) 170 µm, (b) 130 −160 µm, and (c) multilayer structure of 85 −115 µm glass, 130 −160 µm air gap, and 85 −115 µm glass. Insets show schematic representations of the samples.

Figure 2 shows the reconstructed axial scans (A-scans). At each measurement point, two spectra, S(λs), were recorded with a relative phase shift of π. Their subtrac- tion suppresses the DC contribution and the autocorre- lation terms, leaving only the interference signal associ- ated with the reflections from the sample. The resulting spectrum is rewritten as a function of the wavenumber k = 2π/λ. Considering the Jacobian of the transfor- mation, we obtain S(k) = (2π/k2) S (λ). The spectrum is then resampled to obtain a function S(k) with equally spaced k-values. Finally, we obtain the Fourier transform of I(z) = F [S(k)] = R dk S(k) exp (ikz).

Fig. 2(a) and (b) correspond to two single-layer glass samples with different thickness, with nominal values of 172 µm and 146 µm. I(z) exhibits two dominant peaks corresponding to the front and back surfaces of the single- layer sample. In Fig. 2(c) we consider two glass samples separated by a distance of 173 µm, which corresponds to a multilayer sample with three layers. We observe four peaks that correspond to reflections from the front and back surfaces of each glass layer, separated by an air gap. Our results are in good agreement with manufacturer specifications.
